samples.summary: Image gate always resolves the host with the local resolver, so exports still fail on the proxy-only machines the new ProxyAgent path exists to support
samples.evidence: `assertFetchableImageUrl` calls `await resolveHost(url, lookup, target)` (line 394) unconditionally for every name-shaped host, and `resolveHost` throws `SystemError('NETWORK_ERROR')` when the lookup fails or returns nothing (lines 264-280). The gate runs BEFORE `hopDispatcher` (line 710-711), so it runs even when the hop will be sent to an egress proxy that would resolve the name itself. On a machine whose only route out is a proxy — the exact environment `hopDispatcher`/`ProxyAgent` was added to keep working, per the comment at lines 486-492 and docs/design/cli.md:952-957 — public DNS is frequently not resolvable locally, so every external image now fails the export with exit 2 before any request is attempted. Neither the code nor the design doc records this dependency on the proxied path.

samples.summary: Each redirect hop can be requested twice and the first (opaque-filtered) response body is never released
samples.evidence: `if (isOpaqueRedirect(res)) res = await rawRequest(target, agent);` (line 724) re-issues the identical GET through `undiciRequest` whenever the fetch layer returns the spec-mandated opaque-redirect filter. The original `res` is discarded without `res.body?.cancel()` (unlike the redirect and non-OK branches at lines 735 and 741), and the remote endpoint is hit twice per hop. The comment at lines 585-590 asserts undici 'hands back the real response instead', which contradicts undici's own spec-conformant `filterResponse(..., 'opaqueredirect')` path; if it does filter, this doubled request is the normal path, and a one-shot/presigned redirect URL would fail on the second issue.

samples.summary: A malformed Location header throws an unclassified TypeError out of the image fetcher
samples.evidence: `target = new URL(location, target).toString();` (line 736) is unguarded. A redirect whose `Location` is not a valid URL (e.g. `Location: http://[`) makes the URL constructor throw a raw `TypeError`, which is neither a `UserError` nor a `SystemError`; it escapes the fetcher, is reported by `outputError` as `{code:'ERROR'}` with exit 1, and thus violates the documented classification for a server-side fault. Every other failure on this path is deliberately classified (`blocked`, `httpError`, `SystemError`).

samples.summary: Non-string `?state=` in the OAuth callback reaches Buffer.from and crashes with a 500 instead of the intended 400
samples.evidence: `consumeWebOAuthState` guards `typeof cookie !== 'string'` for the cookie but never checks the type of `stateToken`. `@Query('state')` yields `string[]` for a repeated parameter and a `ParsedQs` object for `?state[a]=1`. `timingSafeEqualString` then calls `Buffer.from(b, 'utf8')` (line 41) with a non-string, which throws `TypeError: The first argument must be of type string...` — an unhandled 500 instead of the `BadRequestException` this function is supposed to raise. The same untyped value is also passed to `cliAuthStore.consumeState(stateToken)` at line 124.

samples.summary: startCallbackServer creates a rejectable promise before any handler is guaranteed to be attached, risking an unhandled rejection
samples.evidence: `callbackPromise` is constructed at line 371 as soon as the server starts, and the timeout at line 478 rejects it whether or not `waitForCallback()` has ever been called. `runLogin` attaches a handler only after `await deps.openBrowser(oauthUrl)` (lines 253-261), and `startCallbackServer` is now an exported API a caller may use without calling `waitForCallback` at all. Any such window longer than `timeoutMs` produces an unhandled promise rejection, which terminates the process in Node with no diagnostic.

samples.summary: HTTP 429 is classified as a user error, so a throttled request tells agents to fix their input
samples.evidence: `exitCodeForStatus` returns `EXIT_USER_ERROR` for everything that is not 401/403/5xx, so a `429 Too Many Requests` — which the backend does emit (`@Throttle({ default: { limit: 10, ttl: 60_000 } })` on `/auth/github/callback`, `/auth/refresh`, `/auth/cli/exchange`) — exits 1. A rate limit is a transient environment condition an agent should retry, not something the caller can fix by changing arguments.

verdict.reason: The code mechanics are as quoted (unconditional resolveHost at image-fetcher.ts:394, SystemError NETWORK_ERROR at 264-280, gate before hopDispatcher at 710-711), but the finding's substance does not hold under the Correctness lens. (a) Its central claim — "Neither the code nor the design doc records this dependency on the proxied path" — is false: image-fetcher.ts:249-255 states an unresolvable name is a system failure rather than an allow, image-fetcher.ts:464-466 states "The gate itself is unchanged ... proxied or not", and docs/design/cli.md:915-920 plus 940-942 document both the fail-closed NETWORK_ERROR (exit 2) on unresolvable names and that the gate still applies on the proxied path. (b) There is therefore no logic error, inverted condition, missing guard, or mishandled failure: the code implements the documented fail-closed policy exactly. The only alternative behavior — skipping the SSRF gate for proxied hops — is a security/usability tradeoff the design explicitly considered and declined (image-fetcher.ts:468-478; docs/design/cli.md:944-968), which belongs to the security/design lens, not this one. (c) The operative premise that proxy-only machines cannot resolve public DNS is an environmental assumption about deployment, not a defect in the code's logic. Real behavior, deliberately specified, and out of this lens's lane.
